claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can form a stable, coherent nanoscale oxide-dispersion network at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The oxide-dispersion network reinforces the alloy through dispersion strengthening.
The oxide-dispersion network protects the alloy from environmental degradation by acting as a passivating barrier.
The oxide network enables a simultaneous combination of low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
A controlled oxygen-exposure anneal promotes in situ formation of nanoscale oxide dispersions.
Rapid solidification or inert-atmosphere annealing minimizes oxide-dispersion formation relative to oxygen-exposure annealing.
Impeded dislocation mobility increases mechanical strength.
The oxide network slows corrosion processes.
The oxide network slows high-temperature oxidation.
Formation of the oxide dispersion imposes no significant density penalty.
The oxygen-exposed alloy will have significantly higher yield and tensile strength than the baseline.
The oxygen-exposed alloy will have lower corrosion rates or delayed degradation in salt-spray or electrochemical testing.
The oxygen-exposed alloy will show lower mass gain during cyclic high-temperature oxidation than the baseline.
The oxygen-exposed alloy will show reduced oxide spallation during cyclic high-temperature oxidation.
The benefits will diminish or vanish in extremely aggressive environments or in high-water-vapor conditions that prevent maintenance of a coherent oxide network.
The benefits will diminish or vanish below temperatures needed for oxide-network formation or stabilization.
The oxygen partial pressure, annealing temperature, annealing duration, and dispersion size and distribution required for optimum performance are not established.
Oxide-dispersion processing may trade strength or environmental resistance against ductility under extreme conditions.
